query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Q235 steel, corrosion protection during high‐temperature (700–900 °C) salt exposure is governed by the formation of an adherent, continuous oxide layer along refined grain boundaries that develop during controlled annealing. This enhanced grain-boundary passivation limits further oxidation and salt attack, whereas the as-received (non-annealed) microstructure with coarser, less uniformly distributed grain boundaries results in a less stable oxide layer and accelerated degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: Pre-exposure Q235 steel in its as-received, low-carbon state, exhibiting a relatively coarse and heterogeneous grain structure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled annealing process designed to refine the grain-boundary structure and to promote uniform oxidation, combined with in-situ monitoring of oxide scale formation during subsequent high-temperature (700–900 °C) salt exposure.
generation.conditions: Corrosion tests conducted in high-temperature oxidation environments (e.g., molten salt mixtures such as 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl) compared between annealed and non-annealed (as-received) Q235 steel. The hypothesis is expected to be effective under these high-temperature, salt-laden conditions but may not apply under ambient or purely aqueous conditions where different corrosion mechanisms dominate.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary structure and the continuity/adherence of the resulting oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: Controlled annealing refines the microstructure, leading to more uniformly distributed and well-organized grain boundaries that act as preferential sites for the formation of a continuous, adherent oxide film. This film impedes the ingress of corrosive species and mitigates mass change during high-temperature salt exposure. In contrast, the as-received state—with its irregular, coarser grain boundaries—favors discontinuous oxide formation, promoting spallation and enhanced corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed Q235 steel will exhibit more uniform, adherent oxide scales with lower mass change and reduced corrosion rates compared to non-annealed Q235 steel under identical high-temperature salt exposures.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel in its as-received, non-annealed state.
generation.boundary: The proposed mechanism is anticipated to hold under high-temperature conditions (700–900 °C) in aggressive salt environments; it may not be applicable under ambient temperature or low-salt conditions where different corrosion kinetics and protective mechanisms (such as moisture-induced passivation) are dominant.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative effects of grain size refinement on oxide adherence and the role of minor impurities in Q235 steel remain uncertain. Further, variations in salt chemistry or exposure duration could modulate the effectiveness of the grain-boundary passivation mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples: one set subjected to a controlled annealing protocol aimed at refining the grain boundaries and another set left in the as-received state. Expose both sets to high-temperature (700–900 °C) molten salt corrosion tests (e.g., in a 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl environment) while performing in-situ monitoring of oxide scale formation using SEM/EDS and EBSD to assess grain boundary characteristics.
measurements: Oxide scale morphology and continuity (via SEM and EDS)
Grain-boundary mapping and size distribution (via EBSD)
Electrochemical corrosion rate tests if applicable
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed Q235 steel does not exhibit a significantly more continuous and adherent oxide layer, nor a lower rate of mass change and corrosion, compared to the control (non-annealed) samples under identical high-temperature salt exposure conditions, then the hypothesis that grain-boundary refinement and associated passivation govern the improved corrosion protection will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA and co-doping Y and Hf AlCoCrFeNi2.1 YHf-EHEA coatings were successfully prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. 1. The YHf co-doping did not alter the solidification microstructure and phase structure of the EHEA coating. The microstructure morphologies of the top and bottom portions of coatings were composed of cellular and columnar dendrites, respectively. And the phase structure consisted of FCC and BCC/B2. 2. After heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h, the BCC/B2 structure was relatively stable in all coatings while the nanoscale Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC. 3. The grain sizes of the HT-EHEA and HT-YHf coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Additionally, the volume fractions of the LAGBs decreased by 13.9% and 8.3% in the HT-EHEA and HT-YHf coatings, respectively. 4. In this work, we have shown that an HEA film can be synthesized from a single partially spark-plasma-sintered target. Such use of single target sputtering was beneficial for synthesizing nanocrystalline films with low grain sizes and superior mechanical properties. The addition of Cu to the RHEA film was shown to increase the hardness and nanopillar compressional strength. The CuMoTaWV RHEA film showed an average hardness and nanopillar compressive strength of 19 ± 2.3 and 10 ± 0.8 GPa, respectively, which are ∼20% higher than those of the reported RHEA films in the literature. The high hardness and compressional strength of the reported film were attributed to nanocrystalline grain size and grain-boundary-controlled plastic deformation. The wear behavior and adhesion of the CuMoTaWV film on a steel substrate were improved by annealing at 300 °C, and it showed improved coefficient of friction and wear resistance at RT and 300 °C. The reported results suggest that RHEA films can be beneficial for wear and nanopillar applications.

reading.lever: Perform controlled annealing and in-situ oxide scale and microstructure monitoring on Q235 to isolate grain-boundary passivation effects.
reading.why: Because analogous studies in HEA and duplex steels reveal that microstructure-driven elemental redistribution and oxide adherence govern corrosion resistance.
